items.question: What did FLEX find about methanol droplet flames?

result.answer: Methanol burns with a very dim blue flame and produces little soot, unlike heptane. [nasa:glenn-flex] The FLEX study uses methanol and heptane as its two typical fuels. [nasa:glenn-flex]

claims.text: Methanol burns with a very dim blue flame and produces little soot, unlike heptane.

items.question: Can we trust the model predictions for a Moon base?

result.answer: Previous computational modeling suggests that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth. [nasa:glenn-fm2] FM2 is intended to verify whether some materials burning in partial-gravity environments may be more flammable compared to 1g. [nasa:glenn-fm2]

claims.text: Previous computational modeling suggests that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth.
claims.excerpt: Previous computational modeling, bolstered by experiments aboard parabolicflight aircraft and the ISS, suggest that materials may burn at lower oxygen concentrations in lunar gravity compared to Earth.

claims.text: FM2 is intended to verify whether some materials burning in partial-gravity environments may be more flammable compared to 1g.
claims.excerpt: Verify whether some materials burning in partial-gravity environments may be more flammable compared to 1g.

facts.statement: Moon-Base conditions (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi = 527.5 mmHg) sit at the low-pressure edge of the FLEX data: only 9 methanol and 7 heptane runs have oxygen of 30% or more at 620 mmHg or less, so the extinction-diameter and test-end models are not valid there.
facts.caveat: No measured partial-gravity data exists in PSI; these are microgravity tables.

facts.statement: At Moon-Base-like conditions (30% oxygen, 527.5 mmHg, 2 mm droplet) the disruption model gives a 89% chance a methanol droplet breaks apart and 95% for heptane, in line with the data: 17 of 23 FLEX runs at 28% oxygen or more broke apart.
facts.caveat: Few runs exist at exactly these conditions: read it as a trend, not a measurement.

result.summary: The evidence does not establish that the model is trustworthy for a Moon base. Only 9 methanol and 7 heptane runs covered conditions near Moon-Base air at this low pressure, so the extinction-diameter and test-end models are not valid there. The disruption model does predict breakup at Moon-Base-like conditions (about 89% for methanol and 95% for heptane), in line with 17 of 23 runs at 28% oxygen or more, which suggests it fits the data better. Lunar-gravity flammability is still being tested, so the question remains open.

items.question: How do measured burning rates compare with droplet combustion theory?

result.answer: The experimental burning-rate constants were obtained by linear least-square fitting of the droplet diameter squared versus time curves. [ntrs:20130014061]

claims.text: The experimental burning-rate constants were obtained by linear least-square fitting of the droplet diameter squared versus time curves.
claims.excerpt: The experimental Kex values were obtained by linear least-square fitting of the D2-versus-time curves.

facts.statement: FLEX droplets burn well below the textbook (classical droplet-combustion theory) burning rate: the median run reaches about 0.67 of the textbook value for methanol and 0.35 for heptane (257 runs).
facts.caveat: The textbook formula leaves out radiation heat loss, soot and unsteady effects, and the team's gas property values are rough: trust the direction and rough size, not the exact ratios.

facts.statement: FLEX burning rates are burning-rate constants in mm2/s: the slope of droplet diameter squared against time, as NASA's FLEX Detailed Results report (NASA/TP-2015-216046) gives them; the PSI table header shows only mm.

result.summary: Measured burning rates in the FLEX experiments fell well short of droplet combustion theory. The median run reached about 0.67 of the textbook value for methanol and about 0.35 for heptane, across 257 runs. The evidence covers droplets burning in the FLEX tests, not any particular habitat's air or gravity.

items.question: How could ACME research reduce pollution on Earth?

result.answer: The primary goal of ACME is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. [nasa:glenn-acme] ACME results could help create more efficient and less polluting designs for burning fuel. [nasa:studying-combustion] ACME work includes developing and verifying improved computational models of combustion to reduce pollutant emission on Earth. [nasa:glenn-acme]

result.summary: ACME research aims to make burning fuel on Earth more efficient and less polluting. Its results could help design flames with more or less soot, depending on the need, and it includes building and checking improved computer models of combustion. The evidence describes these goals and possible designs, but does not report measured pollution reductions.

items.question: How did NASA help firefighters' breathing equipment?

result.answer: A NASA-related project led to a lightweight breathing system with a face mask, frame, harness and air bottle. [nasa:spinoff-breathing] The breathing system used an aluminum composite material, and its frame and harness were easier to put on and take off. [nasa:spinoff-breathing] The excerpt states that every major manufacturer of breathing apparatus now incorporates NASA technology in some form. [nasa:spinoff-breathing]

claims.text: A NASA-related project led to a lightweight breathing system with a face mask, frame, harness and air bottle.
claims.excerpt: A National Bureau of Standards/NASA project directed by Johnson resulted in a lightweight breathing system including face mask, frame, harness and air bottle marketed by Scott Aviation.

claims.text: The breathing system used an aluminum composite material, and its frame and harness were easier to put on and take off.
claims.excerpt: Aluminum composite material was used; frame and harness were easier to put on and take off.

claims.text: The excerpt states that every major manufacturer of breathing apparatus now incorporates NASA technology in some form.
claims.excerpt: Today every major manufacturer of breathing apparatus incorporates NASA technology in some form, and inhalation injuries have been reduced.

result.summary: NASA-related work led to a lightweight breathing system with a face mask, frame, harness and air bottle, marketed by Scott Aviation. It used an aluminum composite material, and its frame and harness were easier to put on and take off. The evidence says every major manufacturer of breathing apparatus now incorporates NASA technology in some form, and that inhalation injuries have been reduced.

items.question: What is PBI fabric and how do firefighters use it?

result.answer: PBI fabric withstands the dangers associated with firefighting, arc flash, and flash fire. [nasa:spinoff-pbi] PBI Gold blends 40 percent thermal-resistant PBI fibers with 60 percent high-strength aramid fibers. [nasa:spinoff-pbi] PBI Gold provides firefighters and industrial workers with superior protection and meets or exceeds NFPA and EN 469 requirements. [nasa:spinoff-pbi]

claims.text: PBI fabric withstands the dangers associated with firefighting, arc flash, and flash fire.
claims.excerpt: PBI fabric withstands the dangers associated with firefighting, arc flash, and flash fire.

claims.text: PBI Gold blends 40 percent thermal-resistant PBI fibers with 60 percent high-strength aramid fibers.
claims.excerpt: PBI Gold blends 40 percent thermal-resistant PBI fibers with 60 percent high-strength aramid, resulting in a fabric which does not shrink, become brittle, or break open under extreme heat and flame exposure.

claims.text: PBI Gold provides firefighters and industrial workers with superior protection and meets or exceeds NFPA and EN 469 requirements.
claims.excerpt: PBI Gold provides firefighters and industrial workers with superior protection and meets or exceeds every National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) and EN 469 (rating standard for protective clothing for firefighters) requirement.

result.summary: PBI is a fabric that withstands the dangers of firefighting, arc flash, and flash fire. One version, PBI Gold, blends 40 percent heat-resistant PBI fibers with 60 percent high-strength aramid fibers, and it is designed to keep its shape and not break open under extreme heat and flame. The evidence describes its use in protective clothing for firefighters and industrial workers but does not explain the specific gear or procedures they use it in.
